topics.summary: The two questions from the class revision sheet: the skeleton and joints (Q1), and muscles, tendons and antagonistic pairs in the arm and leg (Q2).

images.caption: Q1 (d): part of the arm. Part A is the biceps, part B the triceps.
Q2: muscles and bones of a human arm.
Q2 (c): muscles and bones of a human leg (toes on the left). D = front of thigh (quadriceps), A = back of thigh (hamstrings), C = front of shin, B = calf.

facts: Q1 (a): joints in the leg — **hip**, **knee** and **ankle**. We need joints so the skeleton can **bend and move**.
Q1 (b): the **ribs** move so we can breathe; the **lower jaw** moves so we can chew food.
Q1 (c): **calcium** is needed in the diet for strong bones and teeth.
Q1 (d): parts A and B are **muscles**. When part A (the biceps) gets shorter, the lower arm moves **up**.
Q2 (a): tendons must **not stretch**, so that when the muscle contracts its pull moves the bone (none of the pull is lost).
Q2 (b): **antagonistic pair** — the two muscles work against each other: when one **contracts**, the other **relaxes**.
Q2 (c): **C** (front of the shin) contracts to lift the toes. The antagonistic pairs are **B and C** and **D and A**.

topics.title: Handout: the skeletal system
topics.source: Class handout “The Skeletal System” (Lesson 1). The sheet is blank to fill in — the answers here are ours, so check them against what you wrote in class.
topics.summary: The three parts of the handout: the bones of the skeletal system, the functions of the skeleton (with the benefit to performance), and the types of connective tissue.

images.caption: Bones of the skeletal system — the handout asks you to label them. Hide the names to test yourself.

table.title: Functions of the skeleton
head: Function
Explanation
Benefit to performance
rows: Gives the body its shape and holds it upright; muscles and organs hang on it.
A firm frame for good posture and technique, e.g. a balanced stance in gymnastics.
Bones surround vital organs: the skull protects the brain, the ribs the heart and lungs, the vertebrae the spinal cord.
You can take part in contact sports (a rugby tackle, a header) with less risk of serious injury.
Muscles are attached to bones by tendons and pull on them; bones act as levers at the joints.
Lets you run, jump, throw and kick.
Red and white blood cells are made in the bone marrow.
Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles, so you can keep going for longer; white blood cells fight infection.
Strong bones break less easily; calcium is also needed for muscles to contract.

facts: **Ligaments** join **bone to bone** at a joint. They are strong and slightly stretchy, and hold the joint together so it stays stable.
**Tendons** join **muscle to bone**. They are strong and do **not stretch**, so the pull of the muscle moves the bone.
**Cartilage** covers the **ends of the bones** at a joint. It is smooth and rubbery: it stops the bones rubbing together (less friction) and absorbs shock.
keywords: smooth cushion on the ends of bones
how a function helps you in sport

topics.title: Levels of organisation
topics.summary: How living things are built up: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

images.caption: From one cell to a whole organism. Each level is made of the one before it.

facts: A **cell** is the smallest building block of a living thing. Every living thing is made of cells.
A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together — muscle tissue, nerve tissue, the lining of your stomach.
An **organ** is made of different tissues working together to do a job — the heart, the stomach, a leaf.
An **organ system** is a group of organs working together — the digestive system (mouth, stomach, intestines), the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels).
An **organism** is a complete living thing, made of organ systems working together — you, a cat, an oak tree.
The order, smallest first: **cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism**. A trick: Cats Taste Of Old Socks.

a group of similar cells doing the same job
different tissues working together (heart, lung, leaf)

topics.title: The skeleton
topics.summary: The names of the main bones and the five jobs the skeleton does.

images.caption: The main bones of the human skeleton. An adult has 206 bones.

facts: The skeleton has **five jobs**: **support** (holds the body up), **protection** (skull protects the brain, ribs protect the heart and lungs), **movement** (muscles pull on bones), **making blood cells** (in the bone marrow) and **storing minerals** such as calcium.
**Skull** — protects the brain. **Vertebrae** (backbone / spine) — protect the spinal cord. **Ribs** — protect the heart and lungs.
Arm: **humerus** (upper arm), **radius** and **ulna** (forearm — the ulna is on the little-finger side).
Leg: **femur** (thigh — the longest and strongest bone), **patella** (kneecap), **tibia** (shin) and **fibula** (the thinner bone beside the tibia).
Shoulder and chest: **clavicle** (collarbone), **scapula** (shoulder blade), **sternum** (breastbone). Hip: **pelvis**.
An adult has **206 bones**. Bones are living tissue: they grow, repair and contain blood vessels and nerves.
keywords: thigh bone — the longest in the body
shin bones (tibia is the thick one)
soft tissue inside bones that makes blood cells

topics.title: Movement at joints
topics.summary: Where bones meet: the types of joint, and the tissues that hold them together and keep them moving smoothly.

images.caption: The main types of joint and where you find them.

facts: A **joint** is where two or more bones meet. Without joints the skeleton couldn't bend.
**Hinge joint** — moves in one direction, like a door hinge: the **knee** and the **elbow**.
**Ball-and-socket joint** — moves in all directions: the **hip** and the **shoulder**.
**Pivot joint** — lets one bone turn on another: the **neck** (turning your head). **Fixed joints** don't move at all: the plates of the **skull**.
**Ligaments** are tough, slightly stretchy bands that join **bone to bone** and hold the joint together.
**Cartilage** is a smooth, rubbery layer on the ends of bones that stops them rubbing and absorbs shocks. **Synovial fluid** oils the joint so it moves smoothly.
**Tendons** join **muscle to bone** — that's how a muscle pulls on a bone to move it (more in the next topic).

topics.title: Muscles and antagonistic pairs
topics.summary: How muscles move bones by pulling, why they come in pairs, and the names and places of the main muscles.

images.caption: The biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair. When one contracts, the other relaxes.
The main muscles of the body.

facts: Muscles move bones by **contracting** (getting shorter and pulling). Muscles can only **pull — they can never push**.
Because they can't push, muscles work in **antagonistic pairs**: one contracts while the other **relaxes**. They pull the bone in opposite directions.
To **bend** (flex) the arm, the **biceps contracts** and the triceps relaxes. To **straighten** (extend) it, the **triceps contracts** and the biceps relaxes.
Other antagonistic pairs: **quadriceps** (front of thigh) and **hamstrings** (back of thigh) at the knee; **abdominals** and back muscles.
Muscles are attached to bones by **tendons**.

Names to know: **deltoids** (shoulders), **pectorals** (chest), **biceps/triceps** (upper arm), **abdominals** (stomach), **trapezius** (upper back/neck), **latissimus dorsi** (back), **gluteals** (bottom), **quadriceps** and **hamstrings** (thigh), **gastrocnemius** (calf).

topics.title: The microscope
topics.summary: The parts of a light microscope, how to use it, and how to work out magnification.

images.caption: The parts of a light microscope.

facts: **Eyepiece lens** — the lens you look through (usually ×10). **Objective lenses** — the lenses just above the specimen, on a turning **nosepiece** (usually ×4, ×10, ×40).
**Stage** — the flat platform the slide sits on, held by **stage clips**. **Light** (lamp or mirror) under the stage shines through the specimen.
**Coarse focusing wheel** — big movements to get the image roughly sharp. **Fine focusing wheel** — small movements to make it clear.
**Arm** — carry the microscope by this (and support the **base**). The **tube** holds the eyepiece.

To use it: put the slide on the stage, start with the **lowest-power objective**, turn the **coarse** wheel until you see the image, then the **fine** wheel to sharpen it. Then switch to a higher power.
**Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.** Eyepiece ×10 with objective ×40 = ×400.
**Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.** A cell 0.1 mm wide that appears 40 mm wide is magnified ×400.

topics.title: Plant and animal cells
topics.summary: The parts of a cell, what each one does, and the three extra parts only plant cells have.

images.caption: An animal cell and a plant cell. The plant cell has three extra parts.

facts: **Both** animal and plant cells have a **nucleus**, **cytoplasm**, a **cell membrane** and **mitochondria**.
**Nucleus** — controls the cell and contains the **genetic information** (DNA / chromosomes).
**Cytoplasm** — the jelly where the cell's **chemical reactions** happen.
**Cell membrane** — a thin skin that **controls what goes in and out** of the cell.
**Mitochondria** — where **respiration** happens, **releasing energy** from food (glucose).

**Only plant cells** have a **cell wall** (made of cellulose — gives support and shape), **chloroplasts** (contain green **chlorophyll** for **photosynthesis**) and a **permanent vacuole** (full of cell sap — keeps the cell firm).
Plant cells have a regular, box-like shape because of the cell wall. Animal cells are irregular and can change shape.

questions.explain: Mitochondria are the 'powerhouses' — respiration releases energy there.

questions.stem: Which part of the cell controls what goes in and out?
questions.explain: The cell membrane is partially permeable — it lets some things through.

questions.stem: In which part of the cell do most chemical reactions happen?
questions.explain: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like liquid where reactions take place.

questions.stem: Which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which traps light.

questions.stem: What is the green substance inside chloroplasts called?
questions.explain: Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What is the plant cell wall made of?
questions.explain: Cellulose is a tough fibre that gives the cell support.

questions.stem: Which three parts are found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
questions.explain: Cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole are plant-only.

questions.stem: Animal cells have a cell wall.
questions.explain: False — only plant cells have a cell wall. Animal cells just have a membrane.

questions.stem: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria.
questions.explain: True — all cells need energy from respiration, so both have mitochondria.

questions.stem: What does the permanent vacuole do?
questions.answer: stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm
questions.explain: The vacuole is full of cell sap, which pushes outwards and keeps the plant cell firm.

questions.stem: Why do plant cells have a regular, box-like shape?
questions.answer: the cell wall holds their shape

questions.stem: Which part do both animal and plant cells have?
questions.explain: Every cell has a cell membrane. Walls, chloroplasts and vacuoles are plant-only.

topics.title: Specialised cells
topics.summary: Cells with a special shape or extra parts to do one job well: nerve, sperm, leaf (palisade), root hair and red blood cells.

images.caption: Five specialised cells and the adaptations that suit them to their job.

facts: A **specialised cell** has a shape or special features (**adaptations**) that suit it to one particular job.
**Nerve cell** — very **long**, with **branched ends** to connect to other cells. Job: carries **electrical signals** (impulses) quickly around the body.
**Sperm cell** — a **tail** to swim to the egg, lots of **mitochondria** for energy, and a head with **enzymes** to get into the egg. Carries **half** the genetic information.
**Leaf (palisade) cell** — packed with **chloroplasts** for **photosynthesis**; tall and thin so lots fit at the top of the leaf where the light is.
**Root hair cell** — a **long, thin extension** that gives a **large surface area** to **absorb water and minerals** from the soil. No chloroplasts — it's underground, in the dark.
**Red blood cell** — a **biconcave disc** (dented both sides) for a big surface area, **no nucleus** so there is more room for **haemoglobin**, which carries **oxygen**.
keywords: a feature that helps a cell do its job
tail + mitochondria — swims to the egg
long extension — absorbs water and minerals

questions.stem: Which specialised cell is very long with branched ends and carries electrical signals?
questions.explain: Nerve cells are long so signals travel far, with branches to connect to other cells.

questions.stem: Which cell has a tail so it can swim?
questions.explain: The sperm cell's tail lets it swim to the egg.

questions.stem: Which cell is packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Palisade cells near the top of the leaf are full of chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Which cell has a long extension to give a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals?
questions.explain: The root hair's long extension reaches into the soil.

questions.stem: Which cell has no nucleus and carries oxygen around the body?

questions.stem: What substance in red blood cells carries oxygen?

questions.explain: Mitochondria release energy by respiration — swimming needs lots of it.

questions.stem: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
questions.answer: to leave more room for haemoglobin

questions.stem: Why don't root hair cells have chloroplasts?
questions.answer: they are underground, where there is no light

topics.title: Unicellular organisms
topics.summary: Living things made of just one cell: amoeba, euglena, bacteria and yeast.

images.caption: Four unicellular organisms. Each single cell does everything the organism needs.

facts: A **unicellular** organism is made of **one cell only**. That single cell does everything — feeding, moving, getting rid of waste, reproducing. **Multicellular** organisms (like us) are made of many cells.
**Amoeba** — lives in pond water. It moves and feeds by pushing out **pseudopodia** ('false feet') and wrapping around its food. A **contractile vacuole** squeezes out extra water.
**Euglena** — also in ponds. Has **chloroplasts** so it can photosynthesise like a plant, but swims with a **flagellum** (a whip-like tail) like an animal. An **eyespot** senses light.

**Bacteria** — very small, with **no nucleus**: the DNA floats in a loop in the cytoplasm. They have a cell wall (not cellulose), and some have a **flagellum** to move. They reproduce by splitting in two.
**Yeast** — a single-celled **fungus**. It has a nucleus and a cell wall, and reproduces by **budding**. Used to make bread rise and to brew beer (it makes carbon dioxide).
Unicellular organisms are so small you need a **microscope** to see them.

questions.stem: What word means 'made of only one cell'?
questions.explain: Uni = one. A unicellular organism is a single cell.

questions.stem: What word means 'made of many cells'?
questions.explain: Multi = many. Humans, trees and cats are multicellular.

questions.stem: Which unicellular organism moves and feeds using pseudopodia ('false feet')?
questions.explain: The amoeba pushes out bulges of cytoplasm and flows into them.

questions.stem: Which unicellular organism has chloroplasts AND a flagellum?
questions.explain: Euglena makes food like a plant but swims like an animal.

questions.stem: Which group of unicellular organisms has no nucleus?
questions.explain: Bacteria's DNA floats free in the cytoplasm as a loop.

questions.stem: Which single-celled fungus is used to make bread rise?
questions.explain: Yeast makes carbon dioxide gas, which makes the dough rise.

questions.stem: What is the whip-like tail that some single cells use to swim called?
questions.explain: A flagellum whips from side to side to push the cell along.

questions.stem: How does yeast reproduce?
questions.answer: by budding — a small new cell grows off the side
questions.explain: A bud grows out of the parent yeast cell and breaks off.

questions.stem: What does the eyespot on a euglena do?
questions.answer: senses light so it can swim towards it
questions.explain: Euglena needs light to photosynthesise, so it swims towards it.

questions.stem: Why does an amoeba have a contractile vacuole?
questions.explain: Water keeps moving in from the pond, so the vacuole pumps it out.

questions.stem: Bacteria have a nucleus like animal cells.
questions.explain: False — bacteria have no nucleus; their DNA is a loose loop in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A unicellular organism can feed, move, grow and reproduce using just one cell.
questions.explain: True — that single cell does every job.

questions.stem: How do bacteria reproduce?
questions.explain: One bacterium divides into two identical cells — very quickly in the right conditions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a unicellular organism?
questions.explain: An amoeba is one cell. The others are made of many cells.

topics.title: Diffusion
topics.summary: How particles spread out from where there are lots of them to where there are few — and why that matters for cells.

images.caption: Particles spread out from a high concentration to a low concentration until they are evenly mixed.

facts: **Diffusion** is the **net movement of particles** from an area of **high concentration** to an area of **low concentration** — from where there are lots to where there are few.
It happens because particles in liquids and gases are always **moving randomly**. Over time they spread out until they are **evenly mixed**.
Diffusion is **passive** — it needs **no energy** from the cell.
The difference in concentration is the **concentration gradient**. A **bigger** difference means **faster** diffusion.
Diffusion is also faster when it's **warmer** (particles move faster), over a **shorter distance**, and with a **larger surface area**.
Examples: **oxygen** diffuses from the lungs into the blood; **carbon dioxide** diffuses out of the blood into the lungs; glucose diffuses from the gut into the blood; a smell spreads across a room.
Cells get what they need (oxygen, glucose) and get rid of waste (carbon dioxide) by diffusion across the **cell membrane**.
keywords: net movement of particles from high to low concentration
how many particles are in a space
the difference between high and low
the overall direction most particles go

questions.stem: What is the name for the movement of particles from a high concentration to a low concentration?
questions.explain: Diffusion — particles spread from where there are many to where there are few.

questions.stem: In diffusion, particles move from …
questions.explain: From where there are lots of them to where there are few.

questions.stem: Diffusion needs energy from the cell.
questions.explain: False — diffusion is passive. The particles are moving anyway.

questions.stem: Why does diffusion happen?
questions.answer: particles move randomly all the time, so they spread out
choices: particles are attracted to empty space
questions.explain: Random movement means over time particles end up evenly spread.

questions.stem: What happens to the rate of diffusion when it gets warmer?
questions.explain: Warmer particles move faster, so they spread faster.

questions.stem: A bigger difference in concentration makes diffusion …
questions.explain: A steeper concentration gradient means faster diffusion.

questions.stem: The difference in concentration between two areas is called the concentration …
questions.explain: Concentration gradient — the bigger it is, the faster the diffusion.

questions.stem: Which gas diffuses from the lungs into the blood?
questions.explain: Oxygen is high in the air in the lungs and low in the blood, so it diffuses in.

questions.stem: Which gas diffuses out of the blood into the lungs to be breathed out?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration — it leaves the blood by diffusion.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of diffusion?
questions.answer: the smell of perfume spreading across a room
questions.explain: The perfume particles spread from high concentration (the bottle) to low (the rest of the room).

questions.stem: What does 'net movement' mean?
questions.answer: the overall direction most particles move in
questions.explain: Particles move both ways, but more go from high to low — that's the net movement.

questions.stem: Why does a larger surface area speed up diffusion?
questions.answer: there is more space for particles to cross at once
questions.explain: Root hair cells and lungs have big surface areas for this reason.

questions.stem: Diffusion stops once the particles are evenly spread out.
questions.explain: True — the particles keep moving, but there is no longer any net movement.

questions.stem: Diffusion is slower over a …
questions.explain: The further particles have to travel, the longer it takes.
